name: Spirit (MER-A)
short_status: Landed in Gusev Crater on 4 January 2004 for a 90-sol mission and worked 2,210 sols. Its last downlink came on 22 March 2010; NASA closed the recovery on 25 May 2011, and nothing had answered by 23 August 2026.
tagline: NASA · United States · Rover · 2004 · The long occupation Ended
stats: sols worked, against a 90-sol design life
driven, the last 0.57 m of it in a year of failed escapes
silica in the soil its dead wheel churned up

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 10 June 2003 at 17:58:47 UTC (10:58:47 PDT) from Space Launch Complex 17A at Cape Canaveral, Florida. NASA's mission page names the vehicle a Delta 7925-9.5 (no. D298) and gives the launch time as 17:58:47 UTC; NSSDCA calls it a standard Delta II 7925 and times it at 17:58:46.773 UT. A PAM-D upper stage performed the trans-Mars injection out of a parking orbit of about 163 by 4,762 km at 28.5 degrees. The full launch stack, cruise stage included, was 1,062 kg. Its twin Opportunity followed about a month later.

facts.label: Where the names came from
facts.value: NASA and the Lego Company, working with the Planetary Society, ran a contest to name the two rovers and took nearly 10,000 entries. The winner was announced on 8 June 2003: Sofi Collis, nine years old, of Scottsdale, Arizona, born in Siberia and adopted at the age of two. Her essay, which she read out at Kennedy Space Center, was: “I used to live in an orphanage. It was dark and cold and lonely. At night, I looked up at the sparkly sky and felt better. I dreamed I could fly there. In America, I can make all my dreams come true. Thank you for the 'Spirit' and the 'Opportunity.'”

facts.label: The rover
facts.value: 185 kg, about the size of a golf cart, six wheels on a rocker-bogie suspension, solar arrays generating up to 140 W on the surface, a top speed of about 3.75 cm per second and a design tolerance of 45 degrees of tilt with a 30-degree operating limit. The science payload, called Athena, was a panoramic camera and a miniature thermal emission spectrometer on a mast, plus four tools on a robotic arm: an alpha particle X-ray spectrometer, a Mössbauer spectrometer, a microscopic imager and a rock abrasion tool.

facts.label: Entry, descent and landing
facts.value: Aeroshell braking, a parachute at roughly 6 to 7.5 km altitude on NASA's mission-page account (the pre-launch press kit instead puts parachute deployment at about 8.5 km), heat shield release, a bridle lowering the lander, then four airbags inflating and, after them, retrorockets that fired until the lander hung about 8.5 m off the ground. NASA's account has the package hitting at about 14 m/s, bouncing 28 times and rolling to a stop between 250 and 300 m from the point of first impact, at 14.5692 degrees south and 175.4729 degrees east, about 13.4 km (8 miles) from the planned target. The airbags retracted, the four petals opened, and about an hour and a half after landing the rover deployed its solar panels and began relaying through Mars Odyssey. NSSDCA gives 14.572 S, 175.478 E for the same landing, roughly 300 m away, and puts the targeted ellipse at 96 by 19 km oriented at 76 degrees and centred on 14.82 S, 175.15 E; the pre-launch press kit instead describes the target ellipse as 78 by 10.4 km near the centre of Gusev, and we have found no NASA document that reconciles the two.

facts.label: What the landing time actually measures
facts.value: NSSDCA gives the landing as 04:35 UTC on 4 January 2004 and states outright that this is Earth-received time. The one-way light time from Mars that day was 9.46 minutes, the figure NASA's landing press kit gives, so the touchdown itself happened roughly nine and a half minutes before the timestamp that is usually quoted. The same catalogue records an entry mass of 827 kg at about 19,300 km/h, and the rover driving off its lander on 15 January 2004 at 08:41 UT. In Pacific time the landing was 20:35 PST on 3 January, which is why some accounts date Spirit's arrival a day earlier than others.

facts.label: The plan, and the price
facts.value: A prime mission of 90 Martian sols, about 92 Earth days, ending around 4 April 2004. Gusev was chosen because it is a 150 km crater with a 900 km channel, Ma'adim Vallis, running into it from the southern highlands, which made it look like a former lake floor. One-way light time on landing day was 9.46 minutes. The two-rover programme cost roughly $820 million: about $645 million for spacecraft development and instruments, $100 million for the launches and $75 million for operations and science processing, in the figures published before the landings.

facts.label: Sol 18: the flash anomaly
facts.value: On 21 January 2004, sol 18, the morning downlink went spotty and cut out 14 minutes early. Over the next three days Spirit answered some commands and not others, sent the same telemetry packet repeatedly, gave one orbiter two minutes and twenty seconds of nothing but pseudo-noise code, and would not shut down at night, draining its batteries. The project manager told reporters there was a very serious anomaly, and at a later press conference called the rover's condition critical. Three flight-software resets had occurred on sol 18 alone, and by sol 20 the team knew it was in a continuous delayed-reset loop.

facts.label: Sol 18: the root cause
facts.value: A design error in a bundled DOS file-system library. Deleting a file freed its space on the flash but never freed the RAM used to represent it, so the memory needed to mount the file system grew with the highest number of files a directory had ever held. The number it currently held made no difference. Two configuration parameters compounded it: the library was permitted to expand its private memory area from free system memory with no ceiling, and when an allocation finally failed the requesting task was silently suspended rather than returning an error. A health monitor detected the suspended task and forced a reset; on reboot the file system was mounted again and the loop closed. The suspended task also held a semaphore the shutdown logic needed, which is why a solar-powered rover could not turn itself off.

facts.label: Sol 18: the rescue
facts.value: A hardware command called crippled mode, processed by the electronics rather than the flight software, told the rover to initialise without using the flash file system at all. It was sent on sol 21, about twelve hours before Opportunity was due to land on the other side of the planet, and it worked. Over the next eleven sols the team recalibrated the high-gain antenna, deleted obsolete data products left over from the launch software load, then erased the flash in small chunks while checking both copies of the flight software after each one, and rebuilt the file system. Spirit was restored to normal on sol 32 and doing science on sol 33. Reeves and Neilson credit the idea for crippled mode to Mars Pathfinder and write that without it the mission may well have been lost.

facts.label: The right front wheel
facts.value: The right front wheel became inoperable on sol 779, 13 March 2006. Spirit drove on five wheels from then on, mostly backwards, dragging the dead sixth through the soil. It stirred once more in December 2009: a resistance test on sol 2113 showed, surprisingly, normal motor continuity, and on sol 2117 the wheel revolved normally through three of four drive segments before stopping in the fourth. By then the right rear wheel had failed too, and the project had found a negative voltage on the single-point ground where none should be, suggesting an electrical short to the chassis and putting the rover's motor controller board under suspicion.

facts.label: The 2007 dust storm
facts.value: In July and August 2007 a planet-scale dust event nearly ended both rovers. Spirit's measurement of atmospheric opacity, tau, hit a record 4.738 on sol 1265, 25 July 2007, and its solar array output fell to a matching record low of 261 watt-hours a sol. Science was cut to almost nothing for weeks. Dust settling out of the clearing sky then landed on the panels, so the recovery in power lagged the recovery in the weather. On 1 October 2007 the rover entered the fifth extension of its original mission.

facts.label: The silica
facts.value: Steve Ruff of Arizona State University proposed pointing the miniature thermal emission spectrometer at soil the dragging wheel had overturned near Home Plate; the spectrum showed a high silica content, and in May 2007 Spirit was driven close enough to touch it with the alpha particle X-ray spectrometer. The reading was about 90 per cent pure silica, non-crystalline, with no detectable quartz. NASA announced it on 21 May 2007. Steve Squyres, principal investigator: “You could hear people gasp in astonishment.” The patch was named Gertrude Weise for a player in the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League. Spirit had worked within about 50 yards of it for more than 18 months without noticing.

facts.label: What the silica might mean
facts.value: NASA's 2007 release offered two routes to a deposit that concentrated: soil attacked by acid vapours from volcanic activity in the presence of water, or precipitation from hot spring fluids. In November 2016, Steven Ruff and Jack Farmer published a reanalysis in Nature Communications arguing that the nodular and millimetre-scale digitate shapes in the Martian silica closely match structures in the hot spring and geyser discharge channels at El Tatio in northern Chile, where halite-encrusted silica gives the best infrared match yet to Spirit's spectra, and where the equivalent forms are built by a combination of biological and non-biological processes. Their claim is carefully bounded: fully abiotic origins are not ruled out, but the Martian structures satisfy an a priori definition of potential biosignatures.

facts.label: Troy
facts.value: Driving south along the west side of Home Plate, Spirit's wheels broke through a thin crust into loose, bright, slippery sand. JPL's updates record drives on sols 1886, 1889, 1891 and 1892 (23, 26, 28 and 29 April 2009) totalling about three metres, and date the embedding itself to sol 1899, 6 May 2009, when the left middle wheel stalled. The rover was left in loose, soft ground with a real risk of being high-centred on a small mound of rocks under its belly, in soil that analysis showed to contain differing amounts of ferric sulfate, calcium sulfate, silica and other constituents. Extrication attempts ran from November 2009 to February 2010 and gained centimetres at a time.

facts.label: The fourth winter and the last downlink
facts.value: The last commanded movement was on sol 2169, 8 February 2010, an attempt to lift one side of the suspension for northerly tilt; very little change was achieved. The last downlink came on sol 2210, 22 March 2010: Spirit still under master sequence control, all systems green, energy production down to 134 watt-hours a sol, and the solid-state power amplifier at a record low of minus 41.5 degrees Celsius. A change in the behaviour of the battery survival heaters had been noticed a week earlier and was still being investigated. Total odometry stood at 7,730.50 metres and never moved again.

facts.label: How it ended, and where it stands in 2026
facts.value: Spirit drove 7.73 km, which JPL's end-of-mission release calls more than 12 times the goal set for the mission, returned more than 124,000 images, ground the surfaces off 15 rock targets and scoured 92 more with a brush. The same release records the climb up Husband Hill as the first summit of a hill on another planet by a robot, on slopes of up to 30 degrees, and notes that nearly a kilometre of the total was driven after the right front wheel stopped working in 2006. NASA ended operational planning and declared the mission complete on 25 May 2011. Checked again on 23 August 2026, NASA still records the mission as complete, and we found no report from any source, of any date, of a signal from Spirit since 22 March 2010.

timeline: Launch at 17:58:47 UTC from Space Launch Complex 17A at Cape Canaveral on a Delta 7925-9.5 with a PAM-D upper stage, two days after NASA announced that a nine-year-old essay contest winner had named the two rovers Spirit and Opportunity.

Touchdown in Gusev Crater. The airbag-wrapped lander hits at about 14 m/s, bounces 28 times and rolls 250 to 300 m, coming to rest about 13.4 km from the aim point. The station is named for the crew of Columbia. The 04:35 UTC timestamp is Earth-received time; the landing itself happened about 9.5 minutes earlier.

Sol 18 to sol 33. A file-system bug drives Spirit into a reboot loop it cannot shut down out of, and the project manager calls its condition critical. A hardware crippled-mode command on sol 21, hours before Opportunity lands, stops the loop. Eleven sols of surgery follow, the flash is erased and reformatted, and normal science resumes on sol 33.
Passing dust devils sweep the solar panels clean, lifting the arrays from about 60 per cent of their clean output to 93 per cent. It is the single event that most extends the mission.

Spirit reaches the summit of Husband Hill, on NASA's dating, and shoots a 360-degree colour panorama from the top. NASA's end-of-mission release describes it as the first robot to summit a hill on another planet, having climbed slopes of up to 30 degrees to get there.

Sol 779: the right front wheel becomes inoperable. From here Spirit drives on five wheels, mostly in reverse, ploughing a trench through the soil with the sixth. It is the failure that produces the mission's biggest discovery.

NASA announces that soil churned up by the dead wheel near Home Plate is about 90 per cent pure silica, non-crystalline, with no detectable quartz. The patch is named Gertrude Weise. Spirit had been working within about fifty yards of it for more than eighteen months without noticing.

Sol 1265: at the height of the global dust storm, Spirit measures a record atmospheric opacity of 4.738 and its solar arrays produce a record-low 261 watt-hours. Both rovers spend weeks doing almost nothing but surviving.

Spirit's wheels break through a sulfate-rich crust into soft sand beside Home Plate. Four short drives over the next week gain about three metres in total, and on sol 1899 the left middle wheel stalls. The rover never moves meaningfully again. The site is named Troy.

After many failed attempts to move the rover, NASA gives up on freeing Spirit and reformulates the mission around a stationary science platform. One new goal is to track tiny wobbles in the rotation of Mars for clues to whether its core is liquid or solid. The remaining energy is spent trying to tilt the panels north. In the end the desired tilt was not achieved.

Sol 2210: the last downlink. Spirit is under master sequence control with all systems green, generating 134 watt-hours a sol, with its electronics at a record low of minus 41.5 C. Total odometry 7,730.50 m. Nothing is heard from it again.

After more than 1,300 commands radiated over fourteen months, NASA concludes the recovery effort and declares the mission complete. The most probable cause of the silence is given as excessive cold that made the survival heaters ineffective. Spirit had operated for six years, two months and 19 days, which NASA's mission page calls more than 25 times its intended lifetime; measured in sols, 2,210 against 90 is about 24.6 times.

images.caption: PIA03275, a polar-projection mosaic that combines a self-portrait of Spirit's deck with the 360-degree panorama the rover shot from the true summit of Husband Hill over sols 583 to 586, 24 to 27 August 2005.
PIA03095, the Everest Panorama: an approximately true-colour 360-degree Pancam mosaic taken from the true summit of Husband Hill in the Columbia Hills over sols 620 to 622, 1 to 3 October 2005.

PIA11758, an approximately true-colour Pancam mosaic from sol 1202, 21 May 2007, showing the bright trench of soil turned over by Spirit's inoperable right front wheel at the patch nicknamed Gertrude Weise, east of Home Plate.

PIA12002, a black and white wide-angle view from Spirit's front hazard-avoidance camera on sol 1889, 26 April 2009, showing the soil churned up by two short backward drives that slipped, with Husband Hill on the horizon.

PIA12203, the Calypso Panorama: a full-circle Pancam mosaic assembled from hundreds of frames taken between sols 1906 and 1943, 14 May to 20 June 2009, from the embedded rover's position at Troy, with the west edge of Home Plate filling the right half and Husband Hill in the distance near the centre.
PIA10128, a vertical-projection Pancam self-portrait of Spirit's deck built from frames taken over sols 1355 to 1358, 26 to 29 October 2007, showing the solar arrays under a heavy coat of dust.

Technicians in cleanroom garments work on the Spirit rover during final checkout in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center on 28 March 2003, with the STS-107 memorial plaque visible mounted on the rover's high-gain antenna.
